notes.meaning: Babylon had just fallen, and a new Median ruler took power. While studying the sacred scrolls, Daniel realized that the seventy years of exile promised through the prophet Jeremiah were almost over. Even though God had promised deliverance, Daniel knew this was a call to seek the Lord in earnest prayer, not to sit back.

Daniel turned his full focus toward God with serious determination. He fasted, put on rough sackcloth, and sat in ashes to show deep sorrow and humility before the Lord. When we see God's promises in scripture, it should stir us up to pray with great passion.

Daniel began his prayer by praising God's awesome power and unfailing faithfulness. God always keeps his covenant—his sacred promise of loving devotion—to those who love and obey him. True prayer starts by remembering how great and trustworthy God is, acknowledging that he is never at fault.

Daniel piled up words for sin—doing wrong, rebelling, and turning away—to show how deep the people's guilt really was. He included himself by saying 'we,' refusing to act superior to his nation. They were completely without excuse because God had sent prophets to warn everyone from kings to common citizens, but the nation ignored them.

Daniel confessed that God is completely fair and righteous in everything he does, while the people deserve only open shame. Because of their unfaithfulness, Israelites near and far had been scattered into foreign lands. Even royal leaders and ancestors had no special shield, since their sins had brought ruin upon the whole nation.

In the middle of his sorrow, Daniel remembered that God is full of tender mercy and ready to forgive. Human rebellion does not change God's gracious character, giving sinners hope to ask for pardon. Still, Daniel did not make excuses, admitting that Israel had refused to listen to the commands God gave through his prophets.

The entire nation broke God's law, bringing down the terrible curses written long ago in the Law of Moses. God did not act out of sudden anger, but faithfully carried out the warnings he had sworn would happen if Israel rebelled. Jerusalem's ruin was so great that nothing like it had ever been seen under heaven.

Even after disaster struck exactly as Moses foretold, the people remained stubborn and failed to seek God with real repentance. So the Lord stayed watchful and brought the full measure of trouble upon them. God's judgments are always just, and hard times should wake us up to turn from our sins.

Daniel looked back to the Exodus, when God rescued his people from Egypt with mighty power and made his name famous. Because God had saved them in the past, Daniel found courage to plead for another rescue from Babylon. Yet he quickly repeated his confession, admitting that the people had acted wickedly and deserved nothing.

Daniel begged the Lord to turn his anger away from Jerusalem and Mount Zion, his holy hill. Because of the sins of Israel and their fathers, the city lay in ruins, and neighboring nations mocked God's chosen people. Daniel appealed to God's righteousness—meaning his covenant faithfulness—to defend his own honor and restore his city.

Daniel pleaded for God to hear his humble request and cause his face to shine with favor on the ruined temple. He asked this for the Lord's own sake, looking ahead to the coming Messiah who makes our prayers acceptable to God. When God restores his worship, his presence brings life back to what was broken.

Daniel asked God to lean in, open his eyes, and look at the terrible ruins of the city that bears his name. He stated clearly that he was not bringing requests based on anything good the people had done, but solely on God's immense mercy. True prayer never claims personal merit; it rests completely on God's undeserved grace.

In short, urgent cries, Daniel begged God to hear, forgive, and take action without delay. His deepest concern was not Israel's comfort, but God's own glory, since Jerusalem and the people bore the Lord's name. When we pray with fervent faith, we boldly ask God to act for the honor of his name.

While Daniel was still in the middle of pouring out his confession and prayer, the angel Gabriel came to him in swift flight. He arrived around three in the afternoon, the hour when the evening sacrifice used to be offered at the temple. Even though the temple lay in ruins, Daniel still marked his day by God's appointed times of worship.

Gabriel explained that he had been sent from heaven to give Daniel clear understanding and insight. God had issued the decree the very moment Daniel began to pray, because Daniel was dearly loved by the Lord. God delights in the heartfelt prayers of his people and is eager to answer them.

Gabriel revealed that seventy 'weeks'—meaning seventy periods of seven years, or 490 years—were set for Daniel's people and holy city. During this time, God would restrain rebellion, put an end to sin, make atonement (a sacrifice that removes guilt and restores peace with God), bring in everlasting righteousness, fulfill all prophecy, and anoint the Most Holy. Traditional commentators see this as the complete spiritual redemption accomplished through the life and death of Jesus Christ.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the 490 years will conclude only when Jesus returns to set up his earthly kingdom, seeing the final goals as future.
Reformed writers often view the seventy weeks as a symbolic period of ten jubilees that was entirely fulfilled by the first coming of Christ.

notes.meaning: The timeline begins with an official decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem and runs until Messiah the Prince arrives. This period is split into seven weeks (forty-nine years) to rebuild the streets and walls amid trouble, followed by sixty-two weeks (434 years). Together, these sixty-nine weeks point to the public arrival of Jesus Christ as the promised Savior.

differ.view: Some evangelicals date the start of this period to Artaxerxes' decree to Nehemiah around 444 or 445 BC, using a prophetic calendar to reach Jesus' triumphal entry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars identify the anointed prince as Cyrus the Great or another ancient ruler rather than Jesus Christ.

notes.meaning: After the sixty-two weeks, the Messiah would be cut off—dying a violent death on the cross, not for any wrong of his own, but for the sins of the world. Following his death, a coming ruler's armies would destroy Jerusalem and the temple like an overwhelming flood. This destruction was fulfilled in AD 70 when Roman armies ruined the city and sanctuary after Israel rejected the Messiah.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe a long gap of time, the church age, separates the end of the sixty-ninth week from the future seventieth week.
Reformed teachers usually believe there is no gap of time, holding that the Messiah was cut off in the final week itself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most modern scholars understand the cut-off anointed one as the Jewish high priest Onias III, who was murdered in 171 BC during the Greek period.

notes.meaning: In the traditional Protestant understanding, Christ is the one who confirms the new covenant with many during the final week of years. In the middle of that week, his sacrificial death on the cross put an end to the need for animal sacrifices under the Old Testament law. Jerusalem and its temple were then left desolate because of their rejection of God, remaining ruined under divine decree.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe the ruler who confirms the covenant is a future Antichrist, who will make a seven-year peace treaty with Israel and break it halfway through.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars generally apply this verse to the Syrian ruler Antiochus Epiphanes, who outlawed Jewish sacrifices and set up a pagan altar in the temple.
